title: Windows and the Message Loop
summary: A Windows program with a window does not ask "has a key been pressed?". Windows tells it, by putting **messages** in a queue that the program reads in a **message loop** and hands to a **window procedure**. This lesson explains window classes, messages, the loop, and the variant games use so they can keep rendering when no messages arrive.
markdown:
## Event-driven programs A console program runs top to bottom and asks for input when it wants it. A windowed program is the other way round: it sits waiting, and the operating system **sends it events**: a key was pressed, the mouse moved, the window was resized, the window needs repainting, the user clicked Close. Windows delivers these as **messages**. Each message is a small structure: ```cpp struct MSG { HWND hwnd; // which window it is for UINT message; // what happened: WM_KEYDOWN, WM_MOUSEMOVE, WM_PAINT, ... WPARAM wParam; // extra information, meaning depends on the message LPARAM lParam; // more extra information DWORD time; POINT pt; }; ``` Every thread that creates a window gets a **message queue**. Windows appends messages to it; the program takes them out one at a time. ```mermaid flowchart LR U["User presses a key"] --> W["Windows"] W -->|"WM_KEYDOWN"| Q["Thread's message queue"] Q -->|"GetMessage"| L["Message loop"] L -->|"DispatchMessage"| P["Window procedure
WndProc(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam)"] ``` ## Window classes and the window procedure Before creating a window you register a **window class**: a template naming, among other things, the **window procedure**, the function Windows calls for every message to windows of that class. It is a callback (lesson 3.04): you give Windows a function pointer, and Windows calls it. ```cpp LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT message, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (message) { case WM_KEYDOWN: if (wParam == VK_ESCAPE) DestroyWindow(hwnd); // Esc closes the window return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); // ask the message loop to end return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, message, wParam, lParam); // default handling for everything else } ``` The `switch` handles the messages the program cares about. Everything else **must** go to `DefWindowProcW`, which implements the standard behaviour: moving the window when its title bar is dragged, resizing, the system menu, closing on Alt+F4. A window procedure that returns 0 for everything produces a window that cannot be moved or closed. ## The message loop ```cpp MSG msg{}; while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) > 0) { TranslateMessage(&msg); // turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages for typed text DispatchMessageW(&msg); // calls the window procedure of msg.hwnd } ``` - `GetMessageW` takes the next message from the queue, **waiting** if it is empty. It returns 0 when it finds `WM_QUIT`, which `PostQuitMessage` puts in the queue, and -1 on error. - `DispatchMessageW` looks up the window's class and calls its window procedure. That is the whole skeleton of every classic Windows program: register a class, create a window, loop until `WM_QUIT`. The next lesson writes a complete one. Some messages skip the queue entirely: Windows calls the window procedure **directly** for them (they are "sent" rather than "posted"), for example `WM_CREATE` during `CreateWindowExW` and `WM_SIZE` during resizing. So a window procedure can be called from inside other API calls, not only from `DispatchMessageW`. ## Messages you will handle most | Message | Sent when | Useful data | |---|---|---| | `WM_CREATE` | The window is being created | | | `WM_DESTROY` | The window is being destroyed | Post `WM_QUIT` here | | `WM_CLOSE` | The user asked to close (X button, Alt+F4) | Ask "save first?" here, or call `DestroyWindow` | | `WM_PAINT` | Part of the window needs redrawing | Use `BeginPaint` / `EndPaint` | | `WM_SIZE` | The client area changed size | New width and height in `lParam` | | `WM_KEYDOWN`, `WM_KEYUP` | A key went down or up | Virtual-key code in `wParam` (lesson 5.07) | | `WM_CHAR` | Text was typed (after `TranslateMessage`) | The UTF-16 character in `wParam` | | `WM_MOUSEMOVE`, `WM_LBUTTONDOWN`, ... | Mouse movement and buttons | Coordinates in `lParam` (lesson 5.07) | | `WM_TIMER` | A timer set with `SetTimer` fired | Timer id in `wParam` | | `WM_ACTIVATE` | The window gained or lost focus | Pause the game when it loses focus | ## The game loop variant `GetMessageW` waits when there are no messages. A game cannot wait: it must update and draw 60 or more times a second whether or not the player touches anything. Games use `PeekMessageW`, which returns immediately, and run a frame whenever the queue is empty: ```cpp bool running{ true }; while (running) { MSG msg{}; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) // handle everything waiting... { if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } if (!running) break; updateGame(); // ...then run one frame renderGame(); } ``` Draining **all** waiting messages each frame, not just one, keeps input responsive and the window behaving normally. Chapter 10 builds the full game loop with proper timing around this. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Not calling `DefWindowProcW` for unhandled messages > The window cannot be moved, resized or closed normally. > [!warning] Forgetting `PostQuitMessage` in `WM_DESTROY` > The window disappears but the message loop keeps waiting, and the process keeps running invisibly. Check Task Manager. > [!warning] Long work inside the window procedure > While it runs, no other messages are handled, and after a few seconds Windows marks the window "Not Responding". Do slow work elsewhere, or in steps. > [!warning] Using `GetMessageW` in a game > The game only updates when a message arrives, such as when the mouse moves. Use `PeekMessageW`. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is a window procedure? - The function that creates a window - The loop that reads messages from the queue + The callback Windows calls with each message for the class - A list of the messages a window can receive > `DispatchMessageW` delivers each message to it. ? How does a message loop end? - When the window is closed, `GetMessageW` returns -1 + `PostQuitMessage` queues `WM_QUIT`; `GetMessageW` then returns 0 - `DestroyWindow` ends the loop directly - The loop ends when the queue is empty > A window closing does not end the loop by itself, which is why a process can keep running after its window has gone. ? How does a game's loop differ from a classic message loop? - It does not handle messages at all - It uses `GetMessageW` and draws inside `WM_PAINT` only - It runs messages on a second thread + It drains messages with `PeekMessageW`, then runs one frame > `GetMessageW` waits until a message arrives, which would freeze the game whenever nothing happens. ? What does `DispatchMessageW` do? - Puts a message in the queue + Calls the window procedure of the window the message is for - Translates key presses into characters > It finds the window's class and calls the function registered for it. ? A program's window closes but the process keeps running. What is the most likely cause? - `DefWindowProcW` was called - The window class was not registered + `WM_DESTROY` never calls `PostQuitMessage` > The loop keeps waiting for messages for a window that no longer exists. ? Why do games use `PeekMessageW` instead of `GetMessageW`? + It returns at once when the queue is empty, so frames keep running - `PeekMessageW` is faster at reading messages - `GetMessageW` does not work with games > A game must update continuously, not only when messages arrive. ? What should a window procedure do with a message it does not handle? - Return 0 to say it was handled + Pass it to `DefWindowProcW` and return that - Ignore it and return 1 > The default procedure implements the standard window behaviour. ```
ideas:
- Read Microsoft's documentation for `WM_CLOSE` and work out what happens if the window procedure handles it and returns 0 without calling `DestroyWindow`.
- In the next lesson's program, add a `WM_ACTIVATE` case that prints whether the window gained or lost focus.
- Count how many messages per second a window receives while you move the mouse over it.

cards.a:
The callback Windows calls with each message for the class

`DispatchMessageW` delivers each message to it.

cards.q: How does a message loop end?
cards.a:
`PostQuitMessage` queues `WM_QUIT`; `GetMessageW` then returns 0

A window closing does not end the loop by itself, which is why a process can keep running after its window has gone.

cards.q: How does a game's loop differ from a classic message loop?
cards.a:
It drains messages with `PeekMessageW`, then runs one frame

`GetMessageW` waits until a message arrives, which would freeze the game whenever nothing happens.

Calls the window procedure of the window the message is for

It finds the window's class and calls the function registered for it.

cards.q: A program's window closes but the process keeps running. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
`WM_DESTROY` never calls `PostQuitMessage`

The loop keeps waiting for messages for a window that no longer exists.

cards.q: Why do games use `PeekMessageW` instead of `GetMessageW`?
cards.a:
It returns at once when the queue is empty, so frames keep running

A game must update continuously, not only when messages arrive.

cards.q: What should a window procedure do with a message it does not handle?
cards.a:
Pass it to `DefWindowProcW` and return that

The default procedure implements the standard window behaviour.
